claim: A DB instance that gets "too many connections" errors is a good candidate for RDS Proxy: applications can open many client connections while the proxy keeps a smaller number of long-lived connections to the DB instance.
question: When is a DB instance a good candidate for RDS Proxy?

evidence.quote: Any DB instance that encounters "too many connections" errors is a good candidate for associating with a proxy.
The proxy enables applications to open many client connections, while the proxy manages a smaller number of long-lived connections to the DB instance .

claim: AWS Lambda functions are good candidates for RDS Proxy because they make frequent short database connections that benefit from its connection pooling, and they can use IAM authentication instead of database credentials in the function code.
question: Why does AWS recommend RDS Proxy for Lambda functions that use a relational database?

values.display: connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy

evidence.quote: AWS Lambda functions can also be good candidates for using a proxy.
These functions make frequent short database connections that benefit from connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy.
You can take advantage of any IAM authentication you already have for Lambda functions, instead of managing database credentials in your Lambda application code.

claim: RDS Proxy bypasses DNS caches to reduce failover times by up to 66% for Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instances, and routes traffic to the new database instance while preserving application connections.
question: How does RDS Proxy help during a Multi-AZ failover?

evidence.quote: RDS Proxy bypasses Domain Name System (DNS) caches to reduce failover times by up to 66% for Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instances.
RDS Proxy also automatically routes traffic to a new database instance while preserving application connections.

claim: For DB instances on smaller instance classes such as T2 or T3, RDS Proxy can help avoid out-of-memory conditions and reduce the CPU overhead of establishing many connections.
question: Why can RDS Proxy help a database on a T3 instance class?

evidence.quote: For DB instances that use smaller AWS instance classes, such as T2 or T3, using a proxy can help avoid out-of-memory conditions.
It can also help reduce the CPU overhead for establishing connections.

claim: During a Blue/Green Deployments switchover, RDS Proxy redirects connections to the green environment once it becomes production, without DNS propagation delays.
question: How does RDS Proxy reduce Blue/Green switchover downtime?

evidence.quote: During switchover, RDS Proxy maintains awareness of the transition and automatically redirects connections to the Green environment once it becomes the new production environment, eliminating DNS propagation delays.

claim: When you connect a Lambda function to a DB instance in the RDS console, you can route the connection through RDS Proxy; RDS then configures the VPC security groups for the function, the DB instance and the proxy.
question: What does the RDS console set up when you connect a Lambda function to a DB instance through RDS Proxy?

values.display: configures the VPC security group for the proxy

evidence.quote: If you use RDS Proxy, then Amazon RDS also configures the VPC security group for the proxy.

claim: Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments are supported only for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL and RDS for PostgreSQL (not RDS for Oracle, SQL Server or Db2).
question: Which RDS engines support Blue/Green Deployments?

values.display: RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, and RDS for PostgreSQL only

evidence.quote: Currently, Blue/Green Deployments are supported for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, and RDS for PostgreSQL only.

claim: A blue/green deployment copies the production database environment (blue) to a separate staging environment (green) that stays in sync with production; you change and test the green environment, then switch over.
question: What is the green environment in an RDS blue/green deployment?

values.display: stays in sync with the current production environment

evidence.quote: The *green environment* is the staging environment and stays in sync with the current production environment.
A blue/green deployment copies a production database environment to a separate, synchronized staging environment.

claim: Typical blue/green changes are upgrading the major or minor DB engine version, upgrading the underlying file system configuration and changing database parameters in the staging environment.
question: What changes do you make with RDS Blue/Green Deployments?

values.display: upgrade the major or minor DB engine version

evidence.quote: For example, you can upgrade the major or minor DB engine version, upgrade the underlying file system configuration, or change database parameters in the staging environment.

claim: The user guide says RDS Blue/Green Deployments support Amazon RDS Proxy and smart drivers, which reduce writer downtime during switchover by redirecting connections without waiting for DNS propagation.
question: Can you use RDS Proxy with RDS Blue/Green Deployments?

values.display: support Amazon RDS Proxy and smart drivers

evidence.quote: Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments support Amazon RDS Proxy and smart drivers.

note: The RDS FAQ still says Blue/Green Deployments do not support RDS Proxy; the user guide (overview and considerations) is newer and is used as current truth.

claim: Blue/green deployments don't support managing master user passwords with AWS Secrets Manager.
question: Can you use RDS Blue/Green Deployments when Secrets Manager manages the master user password?

values.display: don't support managing master user passwords

evidence.quote: Blue/green deployments don't support managing master user passwords with AWS Secrets Manager.

claim: The blue and green environments of a blue/green deployment must be in the same AWS account.
question: Can the green environment of an RDS blue/green deployment be in another AWS account?

values.display: must be in the same AWS account

evidence.quote: The resources in the blue environment and green environment must be in the same AWS account.

claim: After a blue/green switchover, point-in-time recovery history does not carry over to the new production DB instance; its earliest restorable time starts when the green environment was created.
question: After a blue/green switchover, can you restore the new production DB instance to a time before the switchover?

values.display: doesn't carry over to the new production DB instance

evidence.quote: After you switch over a blue/green deployment, point-in-time recovery (PITR) history doesn't carry over to the new production DB instance.
Its earliest restorable time starts when you created the green environment.

claim: Before a switchover, RDS runs checks called switchover guardrails that prevent the switchover if the environments are not ready, to avoid longer downtime and data loss between blue and green.
question: What are switchover guardrails in RDS Blue/Green Deployments?

evidence.quote: These checks are known as *switchover guardrails*.
These switchover guardrails prevent a switchover if the environments aren't ready for it.

claim: While a blue/green deployment exists you pay for the green instances at the same price as the blue ones, so you pay approximately 2x the cost of the workload for its lifespan.
question: What does an RDS blue/green deployment cost while it runs?

evidence.quote: You will incur the same price for running your workloads on green instances as you do for blue instances.
Effectively, you are paying approximately 2x the cost of running workloads on db.instance for the lifespan of the blue-green-deployment.

claim: The RDS FAQ says you cannot use Blue/Green Deployments to roll back changes.
question: Can RDS Blue/Green Deployments roll back a change after switchover?

values.display: you cannot use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to rollback changes

evidence.quote: No, at this time you cannot use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to rollback changes.

claim: After switchover, Blue/Green Deployments do not delete the old production environment; you can use it for validation and delete it when you no longer need it.
question: What happens to the old production (blue) environment after an RDS blue/green switchover?

values.display: do not delete your old production environment

evidence.quote: Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments do not delete your old production environment.
